Regarding your question about which items students should focus on to obtain better grades, that depends entirely on their unobserved ability. Phil

messages.subject: Re: How does MIRT decide loading signs in nominal models?
messages.subject_clean: How does MIRT decide loading signs in nominal models?
messages.body_plain:
The nominal response model is strongly not directional and is harder to control the direction of the final solution (basically, it's hard to tell the software which direction the probability trace lines should be pointing as theta increases during estimation). This happens in all IRT models, of course, but especially so in nominal response models due to their over flexibility. You can probably force the direction by placing a lower bound of 0 on the slope parameter values to at least keep them in the positive direction to force the orientation better, but in general if the solution comes out in the wrong direction you can of course just flip the sign of the slopes and nothing will change. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: multigroup anchor item specification
messages.subject_clean: multigroup anchor item specification
messages.body_plain:
Hi Monika,

When fitting a multiple group model you can really just conceptualize these as multi single group models, but where the parameters are allowed to vary conditional on the group membership. If there were to to be p parameters estimated in a single group, then for a two group setup there will be 2*p parameters instead, where the second set is of the same structural type as in the first group (that's not a strict requirement, but it's the most common for reason of DIF testing and such). Hence, the vcov matrix just doubles in size, where the sampling information for each parameter can be based on one group (if unique to a group) or pooled across multiple groups (as is the case with anchor items). The missing by design effect (coded as structural NA values) doesn't really make a difference here, since missing values do not contribute extra information across groups when the missingness is assumed to be MAR. Even if items were constrained across groups, where on group had entirely NAs for a specific item, the NAs do not contribute to the estimation or VCOV, and therefore the constraints across groups becomes entirely based on a single group (i.e., all strength/information is borrowed from one group).

Regarding your question about the information matrices, the Oakes method is an estimate of the VCOV based on the observed information (negative inverse of the Hessian of the log-likelihood), while the cross-product is also an estimate of the observed information but using the empirical cross product method w.r.t. to the response patterns observed (hence, is not an expected/Fisher estimate). HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Giada,

I believe all you need to do to make the fscores centered at 0 is to center each respective independent variable in your regression equation, and rescale the IVs to have a variance of 1 as well. Modifying COV_11 isn't really advisable as that's really the residual standard error for the model (and changing the MEAN_1 doesn't makes sense since then the residuals won't be e ~ N(0, COV_11), but rather something else and get absorbed into the beta weights; hence, this is ignored by the package). Of course, that might not be the case given that you are including survey weights, which could be complicating the expected values since the item parameter estimates are a function of this weight vector.

Phil

On Wednesday, February 10, 2021 at 9:40:33 PM UTC+1 rphilip....@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Monika,
>
> When fitting a multiple group model you can really just conceptualize these as multi single group models, but where the parameters are allowed to vary conditional on the group membership. If there were to to be p parameters estimated in a single group, then for a two group setup there will be 2*p parameters instead, where the second set is of the same structural type as in the first group (that's not a strict requirement, but it's the most common for reason of DIF testing and such). Hence, the vcov matrix just doubles in size, where the sampling information for each parameter can be based on one group (if unique to a group) or pooled across multiple groups (as is the case with anchor items). The missing by design effect (coded as structural NA values) doesn't really make a difference here, since missing values do not contribute extra information across groups when the missingness is assumed to be MAR. Even if items were constrained across groups, where on group had entirely NAs for a specific item, the NAs do not contribute to the estimation or VCOV, and therefore the constraints across groups becomes entirely based on a single group (i.e., all strength/information is borrowed from one group).
>
> Regarding your question about the information matrices, the Oakes method is an estimate of the VCOV based on the observed information (negative inverse of the Hessian of the log-likelihood), while the cross-product is also an estimate of the observed information but using the empirical cross product method w.r.t. to the response patterns observed (hence, is not an expected/Fisher estimate). HTH.
